text: # Thesis Proposal On Holistic Database Optimization via Leveraging Similarity Across Actions, Workloads, Configurations, and Scenarios > Abstract Modern database management systems (DBMSs) have evolved to support increasingly sophisticated data-intensive applications, at the cost of substantial complexity to configure them for two reasons. First, DBMSs expose a vast configuration space with trillions of possibilities that encompass system knobs, physical design (e.g., indexes), and query options, amongst others. Second, these applications are constantly evolving with changes in data access patterns, query types, load intensities, hardware, and data distributions that necessitate continuous re-optimization. To address these challenges, decades of autonomous DBMS optimization research have produced specialized tuning tools to assist human operators. Deploying these tools involves a complex multi-step workflow where an operator (1) observes the DBMS's behavior, (2) selects tools based on the objectives and their expertise, (3) configures them with an isolated environment, (4) orchestrates their execution to obtain recommendations, and (5) reviews those recommendations before deployment. This cumbersome process results in suboptimal configurations and slow adaptation to evolving applications' workloads due to isolated specialized tools, inefficient reuse of prior tuning knowledge, and the fallible human factor. This proposal presents techniques for addressing those limitations with similarity to enable holistic database optimization. First, we present a holistic tuning tool that optimizes multiple DBMS aspects simultaneously by using action similarity to organize actions into neighborhoods conducive to exploration. We then present a framework that assists tuners in adapting to environment changes by leveraging workload and configuration similarity to re-mix historical knowledge. We propose to extend our preliminary work by transforming the human-centric tuning workflow into an agentic process through scenario similarity. We will first investigate contextualizing deployments and creating semantic tool interfaces. We will then design an orchestrator that learns to select and deploy relevant tuning tools to obtain validated recommendations. With these efforts, the agentic process will enable holistic DBMS optimization throughout its lifetime.

# Introduction

Five decades after the first database management system (DBMS) was developed, DBMSs now form the backbone of modern data-intensive applications. To support the growing demands of these applications' workloads, DBMS vendors continue to release new features and expose more opportunities for end-users to optimize the system for their specific deployment. We refer to optimizing a DBMS system's configuration for a given deployment as database tuning.

Database tuning involves reasoning over the DBMS's configurable options that include hundreds of system knobs [[56]](#page-41-0) (e.g., parallelism, query optimizer), physical design (e.g., indexes, partitioning), and query tuning (e.g., query rewriting, query hints). Furthermore, these DBMS options have complex and subtle interactions with each other, creating trillions of possible candidate configurations [[35]](#page-39-0) that make discovering performant configurations challenging.

To manage this complexity, much of the prior work in automated tuning has focused on specialized tools that target specific aspects of the DBMS. Ranging from simple rule-based tools to more sophisticated machine learning (ML)-based tools, they can optimize system knobs [28, [56]](#page-41-0), indexes [5, [10]](#page-37-0), query tuning [[40]](#page-39-1), and across multiple aspects [58, [65]](#page-42-0). However, these tools make simplifying assumptions or require operator guidance that precludes them from finding the most performant configurations. For instance, some tools use heuristics to prune the search space [[65]](#page-42-0) while others require an operator to curate their actions [[58]](#page-41-1) manually. Moreover, these tools operate in isolation and cannot compose together effectively to holistically optimize a given instance.

However, relying on this cumbersome and time-consuming process limits holistic optimization opportunities over a DBMS's lifetime for two reasons. First, these tools lack principled mechanisms for incorporating prior tuning knowledge. Instead, they rely on an operator's judgement to correctly bootstrap the tool with prior experience. When the DBMS's environment changes, this operator reliance leads tools to take longer to converge and often converge to suboptimal configurations. Second, relying on an operator to identify, set up, and deploy tools results in delayed responses to crises that are inadequate.

This thesis aims to address the challenge of lifetime holistic DBMS optimization. We propose combining machine learning with distinct similarity notions to relate and enable efficient reasoning over (1) actions for holistic tuning, (2) workloads and configurations for re-mixing prior knowledge, and (3) scenarios for automated tool orchestration in response to situations.

This thesis aims to provide evidence to support the following statement:

Thesis Statement: Identifying and leveraging similarities among tuning actions, workloads, configurations, and operational scenarios enables holistic optimization of a database management system throughout its lifetime that improves performance and reduces adaptation time.

Next, we present a tuning tool that leverages similarity between tuning actions for holistic database optimization in Chapter 3. # Background

In this chapter, we provide background on automated DBMS optimization. We primarily approach this discussion within the broader context of self-driving [[42]](#page-39-4) DBMSs that are designed to manage themselves autonomously without human intervention (i.e., holistic optimization across time). We then discuss automated tuning tools and their challenges from both efficacy and deployment perspectives. Finally, we conclude by discussing these tools' efficacy in adapting to environment changes.

# Background > 2.1 Self-Driving DBMSs A self-driving [42, [43]](#page-40-0) DBMS aims for completely autonomous operation that is proactive and efficient. To achieve this, a self-driving DBMS relies on three core architectural components: (1) a forecaster, (2) behavior models, and (3) a planner. Forecaster: This component is responsible for predicting workloads that the DBMS might have to execute in the future at various horizons (e.g., next hour, next day). Forecasting relies on various techniques such as clustering [[36]](#page-39-3) and Long Short-Term Memory networks [[21]](#page-38-1) to predict workload characteristics such as query templates, arrival patterns, and query parameters. A self-driving DBMS relies on its forecaster to guide the planning process, preparing it for upcoming scenarios. For instance, if the forecaster predicts a workload spike in the next hour, the DBMS can proactively scale up to prepare. Behavior Models: The simplest method for a self-driving DBMS to evaluate an action's impact is to change the DBMS's configuration and run the workload. However, this approach is infeasible due to computational overhead. As such, a self-driving DBMS relies on its behavior models [[38]](#page-39-5) to predict the costs and benefits of all possible actions. The self-driving DBMS's design and the behavior modeling framework must be carefully co-designed to ensure that all actions' effects can be modeled accurately. For instance, if the DBMS were to change a configuration parameter (e.g., background task resources), the behavior model must be able to predict how that change may impact both immediate and future queries. Planner: Even though existing DBMSs may suggest configuration changes, they rely on a human operator to evaluate and apply them. The self-driving DBMS's planner uses the forecasted workload and its behavior models to identify promising configuration changes (e.g., knobs to set, indexes to build). The planner then uses authorized time windows (e.g., maintenance window, under-utilized instance) to deploy those changes autonomously.

# Background > 2.2 Automated Database Tuning As Section 2.1 describes, existing DBMSs resort to a human operator augmented with tuning tools to approximate the planner. These bespoke tools are designed to specialize in optimizing specific facets of the DBMS. For instance, a tool may focus on tuning system knobs [[56]](#page-41-0), selecting indexes [[10]](#page-37-0), picking views [[62]](#page-41-2), and picking hints on a per-query basis [[40]](#page-39-1). The human operator first identifies a tool that they want to use. Next, the operator sets up an offline environment, containing a snapshot of the database and a workload trace to optimize. This offline environment allows the tool to freely explore configurations, restart the DBMS, and take potentially destructive actions (e.g., dropping indexes) without affecting the production environment [[37]](#page-39-2). The operator then deploys the tool in the environment, starts it with its required inputs (e.g., actions list [58, [65]](#page-42-0)), sets its objective function (e.g., workload runtime), and then waits for it to complete. Once the tool finishes, the operator reviews and applies the tool's recommendations to the production environment. Although this process offloads reasoning about DBMS configurations to the tool, the operator is still responsible for understanding each tool's idiosyncrasies and utilizing it correctly during the tuning process. Furthermore, existing tools often only target a specific facet of the DBMS (e.g., only knobs, only indexes) in isolation for tractability, as considering all DBMS facets simultaneously results in trillions of possibilities that are computationally difficult to reason and explore over [[35]](#page-39-0). To find more performant configurations, the operator must manually reason about the various tools at their disposal and interleave them during the tuning process to derive an optimal configuration (e.g., first tune knobs, then indexes, and finally queries). This is known as sequential tuning [[65]](#page-42-0). However, sequential tuning struggles to coordinate its pool of tuners, as each tuner assumes it is optimizing the DBMS in isolation. Even though sequential tuning improves over individual tools, it is not a complete solution that enables holistic DBMS optimization over all its facets.

# Background > 2.3 Adaptive Automated Tuning Beyond the aforementioned challenges around their efficacy, existing tools are also unable to adapt to environment changes. As tools optimize deployments, they acquire experience that includes the tool's reasoning, explored configurations, and observed DBMS behavior. Adaptivity captures a tool's ability to reuse prior experience when tuning new scenarios. These scenarios encompass changes in the workload (e.g., parameters, templates, volume), underlying data (e.g., BULK INSERT), hardware (e.g., instance upgrades), and schema (e.g., new column) [32, [57]](#page-41-3). These environment changes are common in practice, with Redshift observing 50% of their production clusters have 50% of queries repeating exactly (i.e., same query template and parameters) daily [[57]](#page-41-3). Despite the prevalence of these changes, existing tuning tools are unable to efficiently adapt to environment changes due to two core design issues: (1) rigidity and brittleness, and (2) workload granularity. Rigidity and Brittleness: This issue is present in tuning tools that rely on cost-based search or machine learning (ML) techniques. For both tool types, identifying only relevant experiences is critical to discovering beneficial configurations [56, 64, [66]](#page-42-2). However, even if relevant experience is accurately identified, problems remain. Cost-based search tools lack a mechanism to apply prior insights to guide the search. For instance, if prior experience reveals an adverse interaction between two indexes, the tuner should prioritize exploring configurations that exclude those two indexes. ML-based tools rely on an internal model to identify beneficial configurations through trial and error. The model's representation directly captures elements of the deployment, such as the schema and workload. Consequently, these tools must re-optimize whenever the representations change due to the environment (e.g., new query, new indexable column). Researchers have proposed using relevant experience to pre-train the internal model [[33]](#page-39-7). However, pretraining remains infeasible due to differences with the target environment and the overhead of re-evaluating prior configurations to obtain performance values for the current environment.

Workload Granularity: Rather than tuning from scratch each time, tuning tools use workloadlevel telemetry (e.g., DBMS metrics) to continue tuning from some historical configuration (i.e., workload mapping [[56]](#page-41-0)). However, this mapping prevents combining individual query insights across configurations. For instance, configurations C1 and C2 may optimize different workload queries more effectively. Without a query-level adaptation method based on query semantics (e.g., plan) [7, [33]](#page-39-7), tools cannot compose the best aspects of C1 and C2 together. Specific to large language model (LLM)-based tools, they overlook opportunities to augment the prompt with targeted experience to guide the LLM's suggestions on a per-query basis. For instance, if a query was tuned before, the tool could augment the prompt with past attempts (e.g., query hints, indexes) as additional context to assist the LLM in generating more effective configurations [11, [31]](#page-38-2).

# Action Similarity

Existing machine learning (ML) approaches to automatically optimize database management systems (DBMSs) only target a single configuration space at a time (e.g., knobs, query hints, indexes). Simultaneously tuning multiple configuration spaces is challenging due to the combined space's complexity. Previous tuning methods work around this by sequentially tuning individual spaces with a pool of tuners. However, these approaches struggle to coordinate their tuners and get stuck in local optima.

In this chapter, we present the Proto-X tuning tool that holistically optimizes a DBMS's configuration across multiple configuration spaces. The key idea of Proto-X is to identify similarities between actions across multiple spaces. Proto-X then uses those similarities to structure the high-dimensional action space into related neighborhoods. Finally, Proto-X synthesizes "proto-actions" to actively explore the resulting space for beneficial configurations.

The rest of the chapter is organized as follows. We provide the key ideas behind Proto-X and action similarity in Sections 3.1 and 3.2, followed by its architecture in Section 3.3. We then provide an evaluation of Proto-X against state-of-the-art DBMS tuning tools on tuning PostgreSQL for analytical and transactional workloads in Section 3.4. By holistically optimizing across spaces that are more complex in terms of quantity and variety than prior tuning tools, Proto-X discovers configurations that improve PostgreSQL's performance by up to 53% over the next best approach.

This similarity suggests that agents should not consider actions alone. Instead, an agent should consider an action and its neighborhood of similar actions together.

text: # 3.1 Holistic Optimization and Action Similarity > 3.2 Proto-Actions and Neighborhoods We combine actions that modify the DBMS's configuration into a holon comprised of multiple fields [[27]](#page-38-3). Each holon field is an independent action corresponding to a configuration space under tuning. We illustrate an example holon in Fig. 3.1 1. K sets a system knob that sets the buffer pool size (shared_buffers); Q-c sets a query knob that disables nested loop joins on Q1 of the workload; Q-e sets a query hint that forces Q2 to scan region in parallel; I builds an index on LINEITEM (l_partkey,l_suppkey). An encoder (e.g., neural network) maps the holon to a point in a multidimensional continuous latent space. We shape the latent space by training the encoder to place holons of similar structure or expected performance in nearby points (i.e., close to each other) [[39]](#page-39-8). The latent space's dimensionality captures a trade-off between the accuracy of holon representations and ease of exploration. Unlike other tuners that directly suggest deployable actions, Proto-X's agent suggests a latent space point (i.e., a proto-action). A proto-action represents a neighborhood of holons with similar structure or performance. Directly decoding the proto-action may not yield a valid holon (e.g., 2 the proto-action sets a integer knob shared_buffers to 519.9). Instead, the agent decodes and 3 searches the proto-action's neighborhood to obtain a candidate set, from which it selects the most promising holon to evaluate [[16]](#page-37-2).

text: # 3.1 Holistic Optimization and Action Similarity > 3.3 Proto-X Architecture > Phase I: Latent Space Creation > 3.3.1 Phase I: Latent Space Creation Proto-X begins by collecting each configuration space's metadata: (1) system knobs, (2) table knobs, (3) indexes and per-index knobs, (4) query knobs, and (5) query hints. A query knob alters the DBMS's behavior by changing a system knob for a specific query (e.g., hash join memory allocation). A query hint injects commands to control how the DBMS generates a plan (e.g., index scan for a table). Proto-X obtains the tunable system knobs either from the user, through a DBMS-specific method, or from externally derived knob constraints [[66]](#page-42-2). For each system knob, Proto-X obtains the min/max values and whether the knob should be restricted to a limited value range [[43]](#page-40-0) (e.g., quantization). Next, it connects to the DBMS to obtain the database schema to identify candidate table knobs. Proto-X defines its candidate index domain by extracting all referenced attributes from the predicates of the user's workload [[47]](#page-40-1) and obtains tunable per-index knobs from the user's specification. Lastly, Proto-X parses the workload to identify query knobs and hints. For each query, Proto-X identifies (1) query knobs based on a user-supplied list or by mining the system knobs for applicable knobs, (2) a query hint for each referenced table that forces a specific access method, and (3) a query hint specified once per-query that forces a parallel scan on a selected table. For example, TPC-H [[54]](#page-41-5)'s Q14 accesses the LINEITEM and PART tables, and thus Proto-X generates the Q14_lineitem_scan and Q14_part_scan hints that control whether the DBMS should use an index scan for those tables. Proto-X also identifies a Q14_Parallel hint. Setting this hint forces the DBMS to scan the referenced table in parallel.

The coordinator handles interfacing with the DBMS, from deploying holons to evaluating the user's objective function on the sample workload. The agent is based on the Wolpertinger Architecture [[16]](#page-37-2), which uses an actor network to emit a proto-action, refines the proto-action to obtain a neighborhood of candidate holons, and employs a critic network to select the most promising holon. In Fig. 3.2 3, Phase II starts with the agent passing the current DBMS representation through its actor network to obtain a proto-action. The representation is either the deployed configuration (e.g., knobs, indexes) or internal metrics data (e.g., tuples processed, pages read) [[56]](#page-41-0). The agent then augments the proto-action with an exploration bias that Proto-X tweaks with small adjustments over time to encourage the exploration and coverage of less promising regions. The agent then decodes the augmented proto-action, searches its neighborhood to obtain a holon set, and 5 uses its critic network to select the most promising candidate. 6 The coordinator deploys the selected holon, runs the sample workload, and 7 evaluates the user's objective function to obtain a reward. 8 The coordinator updates the actor and critic networks with the reward and advances the agent to the next tuning step. The agent and coordinator repeat this process until the agent reaches an illegal state (e.g., an invalid configuration) or a fixed number of steps has elapsed. At this point, the coordinator resets the environment to the initial or a previously discovered configuration before resuming.

text: # 3.1 Holistic Optimization and Action Similarity > 3.4 Experimental Evaluation > 3.4.1 Proto-X Configuration We configure Proto-X to tune indexes and global knobs for all the workloads. We allow Proto-X to extract indexable attributes from workload predicates [[47]](#page-40-1) and to generate arbitrary index candidates. We discuss OLAP- and OLTP-specific workload settings below: OLAP Proto-X tunes 45 system-wide knobs and tunes indexes using all structural rules. We allow Proto-X to build hash, B+Tree, and block range indexes. For B+Tree indexes, it tunes how full the DBMS packs each page by setting fillfactor to 90 (default) or 100 (full). For block range indexes, it tunes the summarization granularity (pages_per_range) by setting it to 64, 128 (default), or 256 pages. Proto-X tunes for each query 12 optimizer-related knobs1, per-table access methods2, and a query hint instructing which table to scan in parallel3. For our maximal query optimization, the coordinator runs supplemental query option sets in the following order: (1) the prior step's, (2) the optimizer's, (3) the agent's, and (4) optional domain knowledge-based sets (e.g., index nested loop join, table scans into hash joins).

Proto-X estimates distribution similarity by sampling 8192 points from each latent space band, decoding them, and measuring the (table,key) distribution. # Workloads-Configurations Similarity

Another key aspect to enable lifetime holistic DBMS optimization is efficiently adapting the DBMS's configuration in response to deployment changes. These changes include the workload's queries, the database size, or the application's schema. Existing automated tuners struggle to adapt and re-optimize database management systems (DBMSs) based on these changes due to their brittle design and reliance on workload-level observations.

In this chapter, we present the Booster framework that assists existing tuners in adapting to environment changes. Booster first structures historical artifacts into query-configuration contexts. On a per-query basis, Booster then identifies the most relevant contexts as references and then prompts a large language model (LLM) to suggest configurations. Booster then composes the query-level suggestions into a holistic configuration [[63]](#page-42-3) with beam search. Finally, Booster provides its findings to the assisted tuner for further refinement.

The rest of the chapter is organized as follows. We provide the key ideas behind Booster in Section 4.1 and its architecture in Section 4.2. We then provide an evaluation of Booster's ability to assist different state-of-the-art tuners in adapting to environment changes in Section 4.3. By composing recommendations derived from query-level insights, Booster assists tuners in discovering configurations that are up to 74% better and in up to 4.7× less time than continuing to tune from historical configurations.

# 4.1 LLM-based Query Adaptation Recent research in LLMs has shown their capabilities in optimization [19, [50]](#page-40-3) and schema understanding [49, [67]](#page-42-4). However, providing curated information to the LLM remains unsolved [[18]](#page-37-8). We provide an exposition into incorporating tuning knowledge into LLMs through four techniques: (1) workload-level prompts, (2) workload-level fine-tune, (3) query fine-tune, and (4) combining enriched query-level prompts with a composition mechanism. Workload-Level Prompts This technique (WL-Prompt) invokes an off-the-shelf LLM with a workload-level prompt that describes the tuning task, the workload, and additional information (e.g., DBMS telemetry, workload summary) as context [[31]](#page-38-2). All techniques utilize experience generated over 12hrs by a holistic tuner tuning a DSB workload where 50% of queries have different parameters. By fine-tuning, this technique improves the LLM's ability to generate more effective configurations for the target workload.

Although this enables the LLM to relate queries to configurations, it requires prompting the LLM with a query prompt. As such, rather than generating configurations for the entire workload, the LLM generates configurations for each query that are then combined into a holistic configuration [[63]](#page-42-3). The technique then uses a composition mechanism to combine the query-level configurations into a holistic configuration while resolving conflicts (e.g., different knob values, conflicting indexes). In doing so, this technique achieves Total Knowledge Remix by reasoning over all available historical knowledge (e.g., past configurations, Internet). To understand their efficacy, we first obtain historical experience by using a holistic tuner to optimize a DSB workload for 12hrs. We then evaluate the previous techniques on using this experience to adapt to a drifted workload where 50% of the queries have different parameters. As shown in Fig. 4.1, WL-Prompt performs the worst as it does not use prior experience. WL-FT and Q-FT have limited improvement over WL-Prompt due to issues around granularity and combining query configurations, respectively. In contrast, Enrich Q+Compose finds drastically better configurations by exploiting relevant knowledge on a per-query basis and resolving conflicts with a composition mechanism. # 4.1 LLM-based Query Adaptation > 4.2 Booster Architecture We present how the Booster framework integrates with an existing tuner to improve its ability to adapt to environment changes in Fig. 4.2. Based on the workload and DBMS, Booster analyzes the repository of artifacts and injects its findings (e.g., start configuration) into the tuner. The injected tuner then further refines the configuration and updates the repository with new artifacts. We next describe how Booster utilizes this repository to derive a holistic configuration [[63]](#page-42-3) (i.e., its findings) for injecting into the tuner. As shown in Fig. 4.3, Booster's operation is divided into three phases. In the first phase, it monitors the repository for new artifacts generated by the tuner and analyzes them for insights (Section 4.2.1). When the DBMS environment changes, Booster uses these insights to optimize the DBMS. In the second phase, Booster receives the user's target workload and the target DBMS (Section 4.2.2). For each query in the workload, Booster identifies relevant experiences and utilizes them to generate candidate configurations with a LLM. Then in the third phase, Booster combines these query-level candidate configurations with a constrained composition mechanism (Section 4.2.3). Lastly, Booster provides its findings to the tuner for further refinement. We next discuss each phase in more detail.

# 4.1 LLM-based Query Adaptation > 4.2 Booster Architecture > 4.2.1 Phase I: Experience Analysis In this phase, 1 Booster monitors a repository of tuning experiences. This repository accumulates artifacts generated by a tuner as it optimizes a deployment. Although these artifacts contain substantial information about the DBMS (e.g., workloads, configurations' efficacy), they are not readily searchable and differ across tuners. To standardize these artifacts into a searchable format, Booster first 2 parses them into query-configuration (QConfig) objects that represent how a query behaves under a specific configuration. Each QConfig includes but is not limited to the relevant schema, the query's execution plan, the configuration (e.g., knobs, indexes), and links to other related QConfigs for structural organization. For instance, Booster can QConfigs together in chronological order if the QConfigs refer to the same query. With these QConfigs, Booster next makes them searchable by leveraging recent advances in LLMs' ability to understand tabular data, schemas, and SQL queries [34, 49, [67]](#page-42-4). For each QConfig, 3 Booster utilizes an embedder (e.g., Voyage 3 Large [[2]](#page-36-7)) to generate fixed-length identity vectors (i.e., embeddings [[45]](#page-40-5)) based on text documents derived from the QConfig. For instance, it can derive them by combining the schema and query plan or by combining the anonymized schema and SQL text. Booster combines these identity vectors with the QConfig and 4 loads them into a vector database for querying in Phase II.

# 4.1 LLM-based Query Adaptation > 4.2 Booster Architecture > 4.2.1 Phase I: Experience Analysis > 4.2.2 Phase II: Guided Recommendation At the start of this phase, Booster is now optimizing the DBMS. Booster receives the target workload and a connection to an offline environment for safe exploration [35, [37]](#page-39-2). For each query in the workload, 5 Booster obtains relevant information from the DBMS (e.g., schema, plan) and uses an embedder to generate identity vectors in the same manner as Phase I. With each query's identity vectors, Booster 6 retrieves relevant historical QConfigs from the vector database, combines them with the target query into the prompt, and 7 invokes the LLM to recommend configurations based on the QConfigs [11, [31]](#page-38-2). As the LLM may suggest invalid configurations (e.g., illegal knob value, invalid index), Booster passes these suggested configurations and the relevant QConfigs through the Sanitizer to obtain configurations for each query that can be deployed. As these configurations target a single query, we refer to them as query seeds.

# Proposed Work: Scenario Similarity

![](images/_page_30_Diagram_2.jpeg)

Figure 5.1: Agent Architecture – An overview of the proposed agentic process. The agent actively observes the deployments or is notified by rule-based alerts. The agent then uses its various capabilities to understand the situation (e.g., diagnostics, knowledge base), orchestrates its tools, and then deploys their recommendations.

We presented the Proto-X tuning tool that leverages action similarity to holistically optimize a DBMS's configuration for a fixed deployment in Chapter 3. We then described the Booster framework that exploits workload and configuration similarity to assist existing tuners in adapting to environment changes (e.g., workload drift, schema changes) in Chapter 4.

As a last step towards autonomous, holistic DBMS optimization, we propose replacing the operator-centric tool workflow with an agentic process that is capable of routine maintenance and crisis response. To achieve this, the agentic process must be able to understand deployment contexts, reason about the tools' capabilities, and orchestrate selected tools to achieve the desired outcomes. For example, assume the Agent has access to a throttler tool and observes that the DBMS is overloaded. Based on knowledge of similar situations or inferring from the tool's semantics, Agent may choose to throttle low-priority queries to improve p99 latency for high-priority ones.

# Proposed Work: Scenario Similarity > 5.1 Crisis Benchmark To properly evaluate the Agent, we first propose developing a crisis benchmark. Related work in root cause analysis tends towards answering user questions [[11]](#page-37-1) or only covers a small subset of crises [22, 68, [69]](#page-42-6) (e.g., missing index, long running query). To facilitate reproducible scenarios, we plan first to create a crisis benchmark built on top of TPC-C [[51]](#page-40-2) and TPC-E [[52]](#page-40-7) for transactional scenarios and DSB [[15]](#page-37-4) for an analytical scenario. We will model the crisis scenarios based on existing work and focus on the following: - Traffic Surge - Read Traffic Spike - Missing/Redundant Index or Partition - Incorrectly Configured DBMS instance - Query Regression - Long Running Query - DDL Query Hangs - No Crisis, Routine Maintenance

# Proposed Work: Scenario Similarity > 5.2 Situational Contexts For the Agent to identify the appropriate tools to use, it must first understand the deployment context. We will first investigate techniques for textually describing the salient aspects of the DBMS state and the current workload. In order for the Agent to suggest appropriate tuning tools, the Agent must be able to explicitly or implicitly identify potential root causes. There is already rich literature on identifying anomalous metrics based on rules or trends and, by extension, root cause diagnosis [11, 61, [69]](#page-42-6). We will assume the existence of rule-based triggers (i.e., alerts) which are common in production deployments. Inspired by prior work [11, [55]](#page-41-8), we will also consider augmenting the DBMS state with relevant information from the manual and the PostgreSQL mailing lists. Depending on the LLM's context limitations [[25]](#page-38-11), we may also consider adopting a tree-of-thought [[60]](#page-41-9) (ToT) approach. Under a ToT approach and taking advantage of test-time compute [[48]](#page-40-8), we envision segmenting the complete DBMS (state, metrics) into smaller pieces based on subsystem (e.g., logging, table changes, buffer usage) and then generating multiple candidate hypotheses with an LLM. By assembling the relevant slice of the DBMS's state and metrics, alerts, documentation (e.g., manual, mailing lists), and a hypothesis, we obtain a succinct context for the Agent to use to identify appropriate tools. We are inclined to believe that including a hypothesis will benefit, but we will also investigate approaches that side-step generating an explicit hypothesis.

# Proposed Work: Scenario Similarity > 5.3 Semantic Tool Definitions Based on the context, the Agent must then identify the correct tools to use. However, existing tools were designed primarily for a human operator. We will investigate techniques for exposing each tool's semantics (e.g., capabilities, inputs, time-to-suggestion), tool descriptors, and situational hints to the LLM. For instance, if the situational context suggests a query is running slowly, the Agentshould select single-query optimization or traffic control (e.g., kill query) tools. By clearly defining a tool definition template, we envision a design where operators can freely plug in new tools for the Agent to use.

# Proposed Work: Scenario Similarity > 5.4 Orchestration Once the Agent has identified the appropriate tools, we must then orchestrate their execution. We assume the existence of a read replica that can be safely detached from the primary instance without impacting high availability, along with a proxy middleware for traffic control [8, [37]](#page-39-2). The Agent uses the read replica's instance to isolate the impacts of its tools. After the Agent finishes running tools, the read replica can be re-synchronized with the primary instance. We will first invoke tools in serial on the read replica. We will then investigate techniques for communicating the tools' outputs to the Agent for reflection [[46]](#page-40-9) as each tool completes. For instance, if a tool identifies slow queries, we may not want to pollute the LLM's context with the raw SQL of each query. Another example is that if a tool indiscriminately builds multiple indexes, we may want to expose the index definitions so the Agent can consider removing some. With this approach, the Agent will be able to dynamically adjust its tool selection as previous tools' outputs are made available. If we adopt a ToT approach, we will also investigate a mechanism that balances investigation across multiple hypothesis branches. A potential challenge is whether these semantic definitions are sufficient to implicitly different situational contexts and appropriate tools. For example, if the contexts are related to problematic indexes, then the LLM should naturally bias towards picking tools that mention indexes in their definitions. In the case that this linkage is not robust enough, we will consider an offline synthesis step where we synthetically generate (scenario, tool) examples. These examples can then be conditionally loaded into the LLM's context based on context similarity to further steer the LLM's reasoning and tool selection.
